cells.tense: You are here, steady at the work, and the change you keep forcing into shape is holding because you keep showing up.
cells.ask: Take a stretch of work that is genuinely ambiguous and run your method through it exactly once, all the way to the end, then read what it produced.
cells.core:
The change you make to how things are structured doesn't arrive in one stroke. It arrives because you keep showing up while the shape is still unclear, and enough light for the next step is enough for you. You build inside the fog and the building holds; that's the whole trick, and people watch you do it without naming it.
So feed it once. Take a stretch of work that is genuinely unclear — where the method isn't obvious and the outcome isn't either — and run your method through it exactly once, all the way to the end. Then read the result. The move is applying it cleanly, not applying it longer. Refinement here is care; it doesn't need to be worry wearing the same coat.
cells.sheetLine: You force the change slowly and it holds because you keep showing up.
cells.verb: forcing structural change into reality, slow but unstoppable
cells.place: moving through uncertainty with only enough light for the next step

cells.tense: You are already bracing for a structure you want forced into shape before it has finished revealing itself.
cells.act: teach what you feel by doing it with others
cells.ask: Take something you are still forcing into shape and teach it to someone by doing it, out loud, while it is unfinished — then let the ending be whatever it turns out to be.
cells.core:
You can force structural change into reality, and the force works — that's not the trouble. The trouble is that you reach for it before the material has shown you what it wants. When the road is unclear, you make the shape come, and a shape made over the fog doesn't fit anything on the ground. Anyone inside it can feel the strain before you can.
Try this instead. Take something you are pushing into shape and teach it to a person while it is still unfinished — show them how it is done, out loud, before you know how it ends. The teaching carries what the forcing can't: you find out what it actually is by handing it over. Then let the shape be what it turned out to be, not what you had already started building.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing the shape before the material has shown itself.
cells.verb: forcing structural change into reality, slow but unstoppable
cells.place: moving through uncertainty with only enough light for the next step

cells.tense: You stopped at the edge of the unclear work, and you are still standing at a door the rest of you already walked through.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Choose something that is still unresolved, and take the smallest real step that begins it — today's action with outward movement, not a plan for the whole road.
cells.core:
Ambiguity asks for a step without the whole road visible, and you have not been taking it. Not because you can't — because the change wants to be forced into shape and you have gone quiet at exactly the point where forcing would work. The work sits undone and you are the one who can do it.
You don't need the shape first. Pick something still unresolved and take the smallest real step toward it — one action with outward movement, today, not a plan about it. Nothing has to resolve for that to count. Doing the step is what restores your sight of the next one, and the change you've been holding back starts moving the moment you begin.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the work and you stopped at the unclear part.

cells.tense: You keep forcing structural change into the world here, and you tell it as though the change happened on its own.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Name to yourself the part of this change you are actually carrying, then feed that drive today by a portion you can keep up — steady, not the whole effort.
cells.core:
The change is underway in more places than one. Someone is pushing it steadily through the fog, keeping it standing past the point it should have collapsed, and that someone describes it as circumstance. The force is there in the work; the acknowledgment isn't. The person doing it is you.
Notice the size of what you are maintaining. Then give it steady care — the change fed today by a portion you can actually keep up with. Feeding is not more forcing; it is the smaller version of what you already do, done knowingly. The direction you keep is yours, and it can be carried on purpose.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the change standing and call it circumstance.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: the Too Little cell locates the person at a door they stopped short of, but the record only gives the seat running on empty — it does not say what is beyond the door or why they stayed, so the cell names the standing-still, never the reason. A reader could reasonably object that they are not undecided but simply between things, and the ask still works there: one decisive act aimed outward, not at the ambiguity. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'Enough light to take the next step, never enough to see the whole road' — it flatters the seat but tells the person nothing to do, so it stays in the preface, not in the cell.
